title: Module quiz: From business problem to solution

questions.stem: Scenario: Quillfeather Retail's sponsor tells the architect that a returns-triage system must be "as accurate as possible" and asks for a design. Which response fits best?

options.text: Settle what accuracy the use case needs and what a wrong decision costs, then build to that
options.says: An unbounded requirement cannot be designed against, so it is made concrete first: "needed accuracy comes from two costs".

options.text: Start from the most capable model and optimise the prompts until accuracy stops improving
options.says: Ruled out because capability without a target spends money without a bar: "cannot be designed against, tested or priced".

options.text: Choose the most elaborate pattern the budget allows, since that gives the highest ceiling
options.says: Ruled out because the ladder buys complexity only for a stated requirement, and the page says "find the simplest solution possible".

options.text: Hold the question open until the pilot has produced some real accuracy figures to use
options.says: Ruled out because the design is aimed at a number, and "the first piece of work" is finding it before the pilot is built.

origin.section: Needed accuracy comes from two costs

questions.stem: Scenario: Pine Ridge Insurance prices three designs for 20,000 monthly decisions. A person checking one item costs 5, a wrong decision costs 250, and the model is right on 99 percent of its confident items. Which handling of the confident items fits best?

options.text: Send each of them to a person, because a human check lowers the error count and so repays its price
options.says: Ruled out because "reviewing the item loses money" where the model beats the break-even, and the page says "Reviewing everything wastes review".

options.text: Pass them through unreviewed, because reviewing them would burn more than the errors it prevents
options.says: The expected error cost of 2.50 per item is below the review cost of 5, so a review loses money.

options.text: Sample a tenth of them for review, since a sample is cheaper than a full check
options.says: Ruled out because a sample is a guess at the same trade-off, and the page asks for design that spends attention "only where it changes the outcome".

options.text: Hold them until the model reaches full accuracy on every slice
options.says: Ruled out because the break-even accuracy is 98 percent, not full accuracy, and a design routes by slice, not by "one number for the whole system".

origin.section: Needed accuracy comes from two costs

questions.stem: Scenario: Corvid Care runs a pilot of a discharge-letter drafting assistant for nurses, who now spend less time writing. The sponsor must say which value pillar the project serves and how it will be shown. Which answer fits best?

options.text: Productivity, measured by hours saved per staff member each week against a baseline taken before launch
options.says: Nurses getting more done is the productivity pillar, measured as hours saved per person.

options.text: Cost, measured by the monthly token bill of the assistant compared with the licence fee that the hospital pays today
options.says: Ruled out because the page says the cost pillar counts "tokens, review time and rework, not model price alone".

options.text: Transformation, measured by the count of letters that the assistant produced during the pilot
options.says: Ruled out because a count of outputs measures activity and not a new capability: "Share of customers served in a new way".

options.text: Performance, measured by the median response time of the assistant for each single request
options.says: Ruled out because latency belongs to the performance pillar, with "95th percentile latency, availability, accuracy by case type".
